title: Count Land Masses
statement:
A map is a grid grid where "#" is land and "." is water. Two land cells belong to the same land mass if you can walk from one to the other over land, stepping each time to a cell that shares a side with the current one (up, down, left or right). Cells that touch only at a corner are not connected.

Return the number of separate land masses. Everything outside the grid counts as water.

examples.why: The cell at (1, 1) and the cell at (2, 0) touch only at a corner, so the top-left mass and the bottom-left mass stay separate. The lone cell at (3, 3) is a mass on its own.
Reading the first row you see two separate pieces of land, but they join along the bottom row. A count that only looks at the rows above gets 2.

hints: Scan the grid. The first time you meet a land cell that you have not seen before, you have found a new land mass. What must you do before you continue scanning?
From that cell, visit every land cell reachable from it and mark each one as seen, so the scan never counts it again. Breadth-first search with a queue or depth-first search with a stack both work.
Count how many times the scan starts a new search. Mark a cell as seen when you put it into the queue or stack, not when you take it out, or a cell can be added many times.

explain.intuition:
Treat the grid as a graph: every land cell is a node, and it has an edge to each land neighbour above, below, left and right. A land mass is then a connected component of that graph. To count components, scan every cell; each time you hit land that no earlier search reached, add one and flood outward from it, marking everything you reach. When the flood stops, that whole mass is marked, so the scan will skip it.

The flood can be breadth-first or depth-first. BFS uses a queue and spreads out in rings, nearest cells first, like a ripple. It is the one to reach for when distance matters ("fewest steps", "how many minutes"), because cells come out of the queue in order of distance. DFS uses a stack (or recursion) and runs down one path as far as it can before backing up. It is the natural fit when you only need to reach everything, or when the answer is built on the way back up (subtree sizes, cycle detection). Here we only need reachability, so both are correct and both visit each cell once. The real choice is about memory: a recursive DFS on a 300 × 300 all-land grid goes 90 000 calls deep, which crashes Python and can overflow a JavaScript stack. Use an explicit queue or stack on large grids.
steps: Set count = 0. Scan every cell in row order.
When a cell is land, add one to count, mark the cell as water (seen), and push it onto a queue (BFS) or a stack (DFS).
While the queue or stack is not empty, take a cell out and look at its four neighbours. Each neighbour that is inside the grid and still land gets marked as water and pushed.
When the queue or stack is empty, the whole mass is marked. Continue the scan.
pitfalls: Checking all eight neighbours. Corner contact does not connect, so example 1 would merge two masses and return 3.

Marking a cell when it is taken out instead of when it is pushed. A cell with several land neighbours then gets pushed several times. The count is still right, but the queue can grow far beyond the grid size.

Recursive DFS on the full grid. A 300 × 300 grid of land is one path of 90 000 calls. Python's default limit is 1 000, so it raises RecursionError; that is why the recursive solution below is marked slow and skipped on the big case.

complexity.space: O(rows · cols) in the worst case for the queue or stack

solutions.title: Recursive DFS (small grids only)
solutions.idea: For each new land cell, recursively sink it and its land neighbours. Short and clear, but the recursion depth can reach rows · cols, which breaks on big grids.

solutions.title: BFS with a queue
solutions.idea: For each new land cell, flood the mass with a queue, marking cells as they are pushed. No recursion, so any grid size is safe.

solutions.title: Iterative DFS with a stack
solutions.idea: The same flood, but with a stack instead of a queue. The visiting order changes; the set of cells reached does not.

followups: You may not change the input grid. How do you track visited cells, and what does it cost?
Land cells are added one at a time and you must report the count after each addition. Why does re-running the flood each time get slow, and what structure handles it better?
